meta.note: SAMPLE STRUCTURE. Every item is status 'draft': check each against official sources, then set status 'verified' and lastVerified before showing it to users. Deadlines and conditions change; this is practical guidance, not legal advice.

title.en: Make sure you have health insurance

summary.en: Health insurance is mandatory in Germany. You usually need proof of it for your residence permit, your job or your university enrolment.

why.en: Without proof of insurance other steps (enrolment, employment, residence permit) can be blocked.

steps.en: Check whether you need public or private insurance for your situation.
Choose a provider and apply; keep the membership confirmation (PDF).
Give the confirmation to your university or employer.

note.en: Needed from your first day; ideally arranged before arrival.

label.en: Make it in Germany: health insurance

summary.en: Many appointments, banks and apps require a German number.

why.en: You will need it for bank verification, appointment confirmations and your employer or university.

steps.en: Compare prepaid vs contract (contracts may require an address registration and bank account).
Activate with ID verification.

summary.en: Everyone who moves into a flat in Germany must register the address at the local citizens' office (Bürgeramt).

why.en: It is a legal duty, and many next steps depend on it: tax ID, bank account, residence permit.

steps.en: Book an appointment at your Bürgeramt as early as possible (slots can be scarce).
Ask your landlord for the landlord confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung).
Fill in the registration form and bring all documents.
Keep the registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung) — you will need it often.

note.en: Generally within two weeks of moving in. Verify the rule for your city.

summary.en: If you entered with a national visa, you must apply for your residence permit at the foreigners' office (Ausländerbehörde) before the visa expires.

why.en: Appointments can take weeks or months; missing the visa end date can put your stay at risk.

steps.en: Check your visa end date.
Book or request an appointment at your local Ausländerbehörde right after registering your address.
Prepare the documents for your permit type.

note.en: Book early; the legal limit is your visa end date.

summary.en: You need an account with a German/EU IBAN for salary, rent, insurance and contracts.

why.en: Employers, landlords and insurers usually require it.

steps.en: Compare online and branch banks (fees, English support, requirements).
Complete identity verification.

summary.en: Check if your university includes a semester ticket; otherwise compare monthly passes.

steps.en: Students: check your semester ticket first.
Others: compare a nationwide subscription with local monthly passes.

summary.en: Finish enrolment (Immatrikulation) and get your student ID and enrolment certificate.

why.en: You need the enrolment certificate for the residence permit, insurance and discounts.

steps.en: Follow your university's enrolment checklist and deadline.
Pay the semester contribution.
Download your enrolment certificate.

title.en: Hand in your onboarding documents to your employer

summary.en: Your employer needs your tax ID, social security number, health insurance and bank details to pay you correctly.

why.en: Missing data can mean a higher emergency tax rate until it is fixed.

steps.en: Ask HR for their checklist.
Send the tax ID as soon as it arrives by post.

title.en: Watch your mailbox for your tax ID

summary.en: After your first address registration, your personal tax ID (Steuer-ID) is usually sent to you by post.

why.en: Employers need it for payroll; you need it for tax returns.

steps.en: Make sure your name is on your mailbox.
If it has not arrived after a few weeks, request it from the Federal Central Tax Office.

summary.en: Every household in Germany pays one broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag); flatmates share it.

why.en: Unregistered households get letters and back-payments later. If a flatmate already pays, you may not need to.

steps.en: Ask flatmates whether the household is already registered.
If not, register online and check possible exemptions.

title.en: Meet people who arrived the same month

summary.en: Join a small coffee meetup with newcomers in your city.

why.en: The first weeks are the loneliest; people one step ahead of you are the best source of tips.

steps.en: Open the People tab and join the list for your city.

title.en: You may get tax back for your first year

valueHint.en: Depends on your income and expenses; people who started work mid-year often overpay.

conditions.en: You were employed in Germany during the year.

howTo.en: File a tax return for the year after it ends (online via ELSTER or a tax app).

title.en: Check if you can join a subsidised German course

valueHint.en: Eligibility and quotas changed in 2026 — check your status.

conditions.en: Depends on residence status; rules changed in 2026.

howTo.en: Check eligibility on the BAMF website or with a migration advice service.

title.en: Free advice on recognising your qualifications

valueHint.en: Recognition can unlock better-paid jobs and some permit types.

conditions.en: You have a foreign vocational or university qualification.

howTo.en: Use the official recognition finder and book a counselling session.

valueHint.en: Some programmes pay a monthly stipend.

howTo.en: Search the DAAD scholarship database and ask your university about programmes it participates in.

title.en: Student discounts you can use from day one

conditions.en: Valid student ID or enrolment certificate.

howTo.en: Always ask for the student price (Ermäßigung) and check your university's benefits page.

valueHint.en: Free, independent help with paperwork and questions.

conditions.en: Offers and age groups differ by service — check locally.

howTo.en: Find a migration counselling service near you.
